title: Why Projects Run Late: Brooks, Parkinson, the Planning Fallacy and Other Laws of Getting Things Done
topic: nguyên tắc quản lý dự án
summary: From the Sydney Opera House to your kitchen renovation: the rules of thumb, and the research behind them, that explain why projects overrun, and what actually helps.
body:
In 1957 the government of New South Wales announced the winner of an international competition to design an opera house on Bennelong Point in Sydney Harbour. The young Danish architect Jørn Utzon had submitted a sketch of white sails. The project was estimated to cost about 7 million Australian dollars and to be finished by early 1963. It opened in October 1973, ten years late, at a final cost of about 102 million dollars, roughly fourteen times the estimate. Utzon himself had resigned in 1966 after bitter disputes and never returned to see it completed. Today the Sydney Opera House is a World Heritage Site and one of the most recognisable buildings on Earth. It is also one of the most famous examples of a project that went spectacularly over budget and over time.

Most of us will never build an opera house. But almost everyone has lived through a smaller version of the same story: the kitchen renovation that took three months instead of three weeks, the report that was "nearly done" for a fortnight, the software release pushed back again and again, the thesis that swallowed a summer. Over the past seventy years, engineers, managers, economists and psychologists have tried to describe why this happens so reliably. Some of their observations have hardened into "laws", short, memorable sentences that circulate in offices and on the internet.

These laws are not laws in the sense of physics. They are rules of thumb, some backed by solid research, some by anecdote and wit. But taken together they form a surprisingly coherent picture of how projects go wrong, and what to do about it. This article walks through the most important of them: where each came from, what evidence supports it, where it is misunderstood, and how they fit together.

## The iron triangle: you cannot have everything

Start with the oldest and most basic idea in project management. In 1969 the British engineer Martin Barnes, teaching a course on time and cost in contract control, drew a triangle whose corners were **time**, **cost** and **quality** (later versions often add or substitute **scope**, meaning how much the project delivers). The point of the drawing was simple: these constraints are linked. If you want the project faster, it will usually cost more or deliver less. If you cut the budget, something else has to give.

The triangle goes by many names, the "triple constraint", the "project management triangle", and countless office jokes of the form "fast, cheap, good: pick two." It is less a law than a reminder that every promise about one corner is implicitly a promise about the others. When a client asks for "the same thing, but by March instead of June," the honest answer is not just "yes" or "no" but "then which of cost or scope would you like to move?"

Modern project management has grown more nuanced. Critics point out that "quality" and "scope" are not the same thing, that the triangle ignores risk and benefits, and that many projects fail not because they miss the triangle's targets but because they deliver the wrong thing well. Agile methods in software development deliberately flip the triangle: instead of fixing scope and letting time and cost float, they fix time (short "sprints") and team size, and let scope vary. Yet the core insight survives every critique: constraints trade off against each other, and pretending they do not is the first step towards a late, overspent project.

## Parkinson's Law: work expands to fill the time

### A satirical essay that became a proverb

In November 1955, *The Economist* published an anonymous humorous essay that began with a now-famous sentence: "It is a commonplace observation that work expands so as to fill the time available for its completion." The author was C. Northcote Parkinson, a British naval historian who had spent time in the civil service and the army. He illustrated the idea with an elderly lady who spends an entire day sending a postcard to her niece: an hour finding the card, another hunting for her spectacles, half an hour searching for the address, and so on, where a busy person would do the same task in three minutes.

Parkinson's real target was bureaucracy. He argued, tongue firmly in cheek, that the number of officials in an organisation tends to grow regardless of the amount of work, because officials want to multiply subordinates, not rivals, and officials make work for each other. He supported this with statistics on the British Admiralty, noting that between 1914 and 1928 the number of ships in the Royal Navy fell sharply while the number of Admiralty officials rose. The essay later became a bestselling book, *Parkinson's Law, or The Pursuit of Progress* (1957).

### What it means for projects

In everyday project work, Parkinson's Law has come to mean something narrower and more practical: if you give a task two weeks, it tends to take two weeks, even if it could have been done in one. People polish, they wait, they start late, they let small extras creep in. A deadline acts less like a limit and more like a target.

The research evidence for Parkinson's Law as a precise rule is thin, and the original was satire. But related phenomena are well documented. Psychologists studying procrastination consistently find that many people delay work until a deadline approaches. And the project-management writer Eliyahu Goldratt, in his 1997 novel *Critical Chain*, gave a name to one version of the pattern: **student syndrome**, the tendency to start a task only at the last possible moment, just as students begin studying the night before an exam. If a task is padded with safety time, student syndrome means the padding is often wasted at the start, leaving no buffer when problems appear at the end.

The practical lesson is not "always give impossibly short deadlines", which produces stress and shoddy work, but "be aware that slack disappears." Goldratt's own suggestion was to strip the hidden padding out of individual task estimates and pool it into a visible shared buffer at the end of the project, which is managed openly. Whether or not one adopts his full method, the idea of making buffers visible rather than hiding them inside each estimate has spread widely.

## The planning fallacy: why we are optimists about our own plans

### Kahneman and Tversky

Parkinson's Law is about what happens once the time is given. The **planning fallacy** is about why our estimates are wrong in the first place.

The term was coined in 1979 by the psychologists Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky, whose work on judgement and decision-making later earned Kahneman the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences in 2002 (Tversky had died in 1996, and the prize is not awarded posthumously). They described a systematic tendency for people to underestimate the time, costs and risks of future actions, and to overestimate their benefits, even when they know that similar tasks in the past took longer than planned.

Kahneman later told a personal story that captures the effect perfectly, in his book *Thinking, Fast and Slow* (2011). In the 1970s he led a team in Israel writing a high-school curriculum on judgement and decision-making. About a year in, he asked each team member to estimate how long it would take to finish the textbook. The estimates clustered around two years. Then he asked one member, an expert in curriculum development, how long similar teams had taken. After a pause, the expert admitted that, as far as he knew, a substantial share of such teams never finished at all, and those that did had taken roughly seven to ten years. He also judged that their own team was, if anything, slightly below average in resources and skill. Despite this, nobody, including Kahneman, seriously considered abandoning the project. It took eight years to finish, and by then the ministry's enthusiasm for the curriculum had faded and it was never used.

### The evidence

The planning fallacy has been studied extensively. In one well-known study published in 1994, the psychologists Roger Buehler, Dale Griffin and Michael Ross asked university students to predict when they would finish their honours theses. On average the students predicted about 34 days. The actual average was about 55 days. Even when asked for a "worst case" estimate, fewer than half of the students finished by that date.

What makes the planning fallacy so persistent is not ignorance. The students knew that previous theses had run late. Kahneman's team knew the base rates once someone told them. The problem is that when we plan, we focus on the specific case in front of us, imagining a plausible sequence of steps, a path where things go roughly as intended. Psychologists call this the **inside view**. It naturally ignores the many unexpected things, each individually unlikely, that collectively almost guarantee some delay: illness, a supplier's mistake, a bug no one anticipated, a key person leaving, a change of mind by the client.

### Hofstadter's Law

The cognitive scientist Douglas Hofstadter summed up the frustration in his 1979 book *Gödel, Escher, Bach*: "It always takes longer than you expect, even when you take into account Hofstadter's Law." The joke is in the recursion: knowing about the bias does not cure it. Simply adding 20 percent to your estimate, as many people do, often still falls short, because the inside view continues to dominate.

## Brooks's Law: adding people to a late project makes it later

### The Mythical Man-Month

In the 1960s Frederick Brooks managed the development of IBM's System/360 family of computers and its enormous operating system, OS/360, one of the largest software projects of its time. The operating system ran late and over budget. In 1975 Brooks published his reflections in a book of essays, *The Mythical Man-Month*, which remains one of the most quoted texts in software engineering. In it he stated what he called, with some self-mockery, **Brooks's Law**: "Adding manpower to a late software project makes it later."

### Why more hands can mean slower work

The title of the book attacks a unit of measurement: the "man-month", the idea that a task requiring, say, twelve person-months of effort could be done by one person in twelve months, by four people in three months, or by twelve people in one month. Brooks argued that this is true only for tasks that can be perfectly divided with no communication between workers, like picking cotton. Most intellectual work is not like that. He gave three main reasons.

1. **Ramp-up time.** New people need to learn the project before they can contribute. During that time, they are not productive, and the experienced people who train them become less productive too.
2. **Communication overhead.** Every new person must coordinate with others. If each pair of people needs to communicate, the number of communication channels grows much faster than the team: with *n* people there are *n(n−1)/2* possible pairs. Five people have 10 pairs; ten people have 45; twenty people have 190. Meetings, emails and misunderstandings multiply.
3. **Limited divisibility.** Some tasks simply cannot be split. Brooks's memorable example: "The bearing of a child takes nine months, no matter how many women are assigned."

### Nuances and criticisms

Brooks himself later described his law as an "outrageous simplification." It is not true that adding people *always* makes a project later. If the people are added early, if the work divides cleanly, or if the newcomers are already familiar with the system, adding staff can help. Some researchers using simulation models have found that adding people to a late project often increases cost without necessarily delaying it, depending on timing and the type of work. Large open-source projects show that thousands of contributors can work productively when the code is modular and coordination is handled well.

But the central warning remains valuable: people are not interchangeable units, coordination has a cost, and that cost grows with team size. Companies like Amazon have popularised related ideas such as the "two-pizza team", meaning a team small enough to be fed by two pizzas, precisely to keep communication overhead manageable.

## The ninety-ninety rule: the last ten percent

A cousin of the planning fallacy circulates among programmers as the **ninety-ninety rule**: "The first 90 percent of the code accounts for the first 90 percent of the development time. The remaining 10 percent of the code accounts for the other 90 percent of the development time." It is usually attributed to Tom Cargill of Bell Labs, and was popularised in Jon Bentley's "Programming Pearls" column in *Communications of the ACM* in 1985.

The arithmetic is deliberately impossible, adding up to 180 percent, and that is the joke. But it captures something real. The visible bulk of a project, the core features or the walls and roof of a building, often goes fast. Then comes the long tail: edge cases, error handling, integration, testing, documentation, the plumbing, wiring and finishing. These tasks are numerous, fiddly and hard to estimate, and they often only become visible once the main work is done. Anyone who has renovated a house knows the moment when it seems "almost finished" and stays almost finished for weeks.

The practical implication is that progress reports based on "percentage complete" are often misleading. A project reported as 90 percent done may be closer to halfway in terms of time. Experienced managers ask instead what concrete work remains, and how long similar remaining work took in the past.

## Conway's Law: organisations build systems that mirror themselves

Not all project laws are about time. In 1968 the computer programmer Melvin Conway published an article titled "How Do Committees Invent?", in which he argued that "organizations which design systems … are constrained to produce designs which are copies of the communication structures of these organizations." The idea became known as **Conway's Law**, a name given to it by Fred Brooks, who cited it in *The Mythical Man-Month*.

The logic is straightforward. If three teams build a compiler, you will probably get a three-pass compiler, because each team builds its own piece and the interfaces between pieces match the interfaces between teams. If two departments do not talk to each other, the parts of the product they build will not fit together smoothly.

Conway's Law has practical consequences far beyond software. A government service split across agencies that do not share data will often force citizens to fill in the same information on several forms. A company whose marketing and engineering teams barely speak may produce a product whose advertising promises features the engineers never built. Some technology companies now practise what has been called the "inverse Conway manoeuvre": deliberately reorganising teams to match the architecture they want the system to have.

## Goodhart's Law: when a measure becomes a target

Projects need measures of progress: lines of code, tickets closed, kilometres of road laid, percentage of budget spent. But measures carry a danger summed up in **Goodhart's Law**, named after the British economist Charles Goodhart, who in 1975 observed, in the context of monetary policy, that any observed statistical regularity tends to collapse once pressure is placed upon it for control purposes. The anthropologist Marilyn Strathern later gave the more popular phrasing: "When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure."

In projects, Goodhart's Law shows up everywhere. If programmers are rewarded for lines of code, they write verbose code. If a help desk is judged by how quickly tickets are closed, tickets get closed before problems are solved. If a construction contractor is paid per milestone, milestones may be declared reached when the work is not truly finished. Measures still matter, but good managers use several at once, watch for gaming, and remember that the metric is a proxy for the real goal, not the goal itself.

## The Pareto principle: the vital few

The **Pareto principle**, or the 80/20 rule, holds that roughly 80 percent of effects come from 20 percent of causes. It is named after the Italian economist Vilfredo Pareto, who observed around 1896 that about 80 percent of the land in Italy was owned by about 20 percent of the population. The management consultant Joseph Juran, working on quality control in the mid-twentieth century, generalised the idea and attached Pareto's name to it, describing the "vital few and the trivial many."

In project management, the principle suggests prioritising: a small number of features often provide most of the value to users; a small number of risks cause most of the trouble; a small number of defects cause most of the complaints. The exact numbers are not meaningful, as the split might be 70/30 or 95/5, and the principle is an observation about skewed distributions, not a law of nature. But it pushes in a useful direction: before working harder, ask which part of the work actually matters most.

## Little's Law: why starting more work finishes less

Unlike most of the laws in this article, one rule used in modern project management is a genuine mathematical theorem. **Little's Law**, from queueing theory, states that in a stable system the average number of items in the system equals the average rate at which items arrive multiplied by the average time each item spends in the system. The relationship had long been used informally, and the operations researcher John Little published a general proof in 1961.

Rearranged for project work, it says: average time to finish an item equals the amount of work in progress divided by the rate at which work gets finished. If a team completes five tasks a week and has twenty tasks open at once, each task will take, on average, about four weeks from start to finish. If the team starts more tasks without finishing them faster, every task takes longer.

This is the reasoning behind the "work-in-progress limits" used in Kanban, a method that grew out of the Toyota Production System and was later adapted to software and office work. The slogan is "stop starting, start finishing." Anyone who has juggled ten half-finished jobs at once, switching between them and finishing none, has felt Little's Law from the inside.

## Escalation of commitment: throwing good money after bad

When a project is clearly failing, why do organisations so often keep going? One reason is the **sunk cost fallacy**: the tendency to continue an endeavour because of what has already been invested, even when the future costs outweigh the future benefits. In a classic 1985 study, the psychologists Hal Arkes and Catherine Blumer showed that people who had paid more for a season ticket to a theatre attended more performances than those who had received a discount, even though the money was gone either way.

At the organisational level, researchers call this **escalation of commitment**. Managers who launched a project have reputations tied to it; abandoning it feels like admitting error; each extra investment is justified by the need to "not waste" what came before. The supersonic airliner Concorde, developed jointly by Britain and France at enormous cost, is so often cited as an example that the bias is sometimes called the "Concorde fallacy," though historians note that the decisions to continue involved diplomatic treaties and industrial politics as well as psychology.

The remedy is to judge each decision to continue by its future costs and benefits only, and to build in explicit points where a project can be stopped without anyone losing face.

## The pre-mortem: imagining failure in advance

If optimism is the disease, one well-known treatment is the **pre-mortem**, a technique proposed by the psychologist Gary Klein and described in the *Harvard Business Review* in 2007. Before a project begins, the team is asked to imagine that it is a year later and the project has failed badly. Each person then writes down, independently, every reason they can think of for the failure.

The trick works because it changes the question. Asking "What could go wrong?" invites polite reassurance. Asking "It went wrong: why?" gives people permission to voice doubts they might otherwise keep to themselves, and it forces the team out of the smooth inside view. The resulting list of risks can then be addressed in the plan. It is a small, cheap exercise, and one of the most practical ways to put the lessons of the planning fallacy into action.

## The bigger picture: how big things go wrong

### Flyvbjerg's iron law

The most systematic modern evidence about project failure comes from the Danish economic geographer Bent Flyvbjerg, who has spent decades building a database of large projects: dams, bridges, rail lines, IT systems, Olympic Games, power plants, buildings. In his 2023 book with Dan Gardner, *How Big Things Get Done*, he reports findings from more than 16,000 projects across many countries. Only about 8.5 percent came in on budget and on time; only about 0.5 percent hit budget, schedule and their promised benefits. Flyvbjerg calls this the **iron law of megaprojects**: over budget, over time, under benefits, over and over again.

His data also show that cost overruns are not normally distributed around a small average. Many project types have "fat tails": a meaningful fraction of projects overrun not by 10 or 20 percent but by 100 percent or more. IT projects, in his data, are among the categories with the most extreme tails. Olympic Games have overrun their budgets with remarkable consistency. This matters because planning methods that assume most overruns are small will badly underestimate the risk of disaster.

### Think slow, act fast

Flyvbjerg's main prescription is to spend more time in planning, when changes are cheap, and less time in delivery, when changes are expensive. He contrasts the Sydney Opera House, where construction started before the design was resolved and the famous shells took years to figure out mid-build, with projects like the Empire State Building, which was planned meticulously and then built in about thirteen and a half months, opening in 1931 ahead of schedule.

He also argues for modularity, which he sums up with the question "What's your Lego?": projects built from many repeatable small units, such as solar farms, wind farms, or standardised schools, tend to have much better track records than one-of-a-kind giants, because each unit is a chance to learn and improve.

### Reference class forecasting

The most influential tool to emerge from this research is **reference class forecasting**, an application of Kahneman and Tversky's insight. Instead of estimating a project from the inside, by listing the steps and adding up their durations, you start from the **outside view**: find a reference class of similar past projects, look at the distribution of their actual outcomes, and place your project within that distribution, adjusting only for specific, well-justified differences.

In practice this means asking "How long did the last ten similar renovations, software migrations or road projects actually take, and how much did they overrun?" before asking "How long will ours take?" The United Kingdom and Denmark have used reference class forecasting in official guidance for transport projects, and the approach has been recommended by organisations such as the American Planning Association. It does not eliminate surprises, but it corrects the systematic optimism of the inside view.

## Putting the laws together

Seen side by side, these laws tell a single story.

1. We **estimate** from the inside, imagining a smooth path, and so we underestimate (the planning fallacy, Hofstadter's Law).
2. We are reluctant to admit the trade-offs and promise everything at once (the iron triangle).
3. Whatever time we have, we tend to use up, and padding hidden in individual tasks disappears (Parkinson's Law, student syndrome).
4. The final stretch is always harder than it looked (the ninety-ninety rule).
5. When we fall behind, the instinctive fix of adding people can make it worse (Brooks's Law).
6. The way we organise teams shapes what we build (Conway's Law).
7. The numbers we use to track progress can be gamed or can mislead (Goodhart's Law).
8. Across thousands of large projects, the result is a consistent pattern of overruns with dangerous tails (Flyvbjerg's iron law).

The remedies are equally connected:

- Use the **outside view**: base estimates on how similar projects actually went.
- Make **trade-offs explicit** from the start, and decide which corner of the triangle can move.
- Keep buffers **visible and shared**, not hidden in every task.
- Define "done" concretely and track **remaining work**, not percentage complete.
- Plan slowly and carefully, then deliver quickly, before the world changes around you.
- Keep teams **small and modular**, and add people early or not at all.
- Design team structures to match the system you want.
- Use several measures, and watch for gaming.

## Applying the laws to everyday life

None of this is limited to professional project managers.

**Planning a home renovation.** Ask friends or neighbours who renovated similar rooms how long it actually took and how much it actually cost: that is your reference class. Expect the last tenth, the finishing, painting, fixtures and snagging, to take far longer than it seems. Decide in advance whether you would rather spend more money or wait longer if problems arise.

**Writing a report or thesis.** Recall how long your last comparable piece of writing took, not how long you hoped it would take. Set internal deadlines well before the real one, and treat them seriously, to counter student syndrome. Measure progress by finished sections, not word count, which is a classic Goodhart trap.

**Organising an event.** List the tasks, but also ask what went wrong at the last few similar events. Keep a visible contingency fund and a time buffer. Resist adding volunteers in the last week unless they can be given tasks that need no training and little coordination.

**Managing a small team.** Keep it small. When a project is late, consider cutting scope before adding people. Check whether your team structure matches what you are trying to build: if two parts of the product must work closely together, the people building them should talk often.

## A note of caution about "laws"

It is worth ending with some humility. Many of these laws began as jokes, essays or observations from a single career. Parkinson was writing satire. The ninety-ninety rule is deliberately impossible arithmetic. Brooks called his law an outrageous simplification. Even Flyvbjerg's data, the most rigorous of the lot, have been debated by other researchers, who argue about how overruns should be measured (from which baseline estimate?), whether the samples are representative, and whether some projects deliver large benefits that justify their overruns. The Sydney Opera House itself is the obvious example: few Australians today would wish it had never been built, whatever it cost.

Laws of this kind are best treated as lenses, not formulas. They do not predict exactly what will happen to any particular project. What they do is help us notice patterns we would otherwise miss, especially our own optimism. The next time someone, perhaps you, says "it will be done by Friday," the laws suggest a gentle follow-up question: "How long did it take last time?"
